title: Reporters Get Subpoenas After Writing About Air Force One—What’s Going On?
summary: Imagine someone knocking on your door late at night—and it’s the FBI, handing you a paper that says you have to go to court. That’s what happened to four reporters from The New York Times. They wrote stories about the president’s airplane, Air Force One, saying that security officials were worried about the new plane’s safety. The stories used information from people who weren’t supposed to share it. Now, the reporters have been subpoenaed (that means they’re ordered to appear in front of a grand jury and answer questions). The government says it’s trying to find out who leaked secret information, not punish the reporters. But many people are upset. A lawyer for the Times said it should “shock the conscience” of anyone who believes in press freedom. A press freedom group called it part of a “war on the press.” This isn’t the first time—earlier this year, other reporters also got subpoenas, but those were later canceled. The president has often criticized the media, and some worry this is a way to scare journalists from reporting on the government. The reporters haven’t said who their sources are, and the case is still unfolding.
why_it_matters: This shows how important a free press is, but also that reporting on secret government matters can lead to serious trouble, like being forced to go to court.

background_read: In the United States, the First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, meaning reporters can usually write about the government without fear. However, when reporters use secret information that might put safety at risk, the government may try to find out who leaked it.

A subpoena is a court order that forces someone to testify or provide evidence. The New York Times is one of the largest and most respected newspapers in the country. Air Force One is the airplane that carries the U.S. president.
Article_Structure: WHO: Four reporters from The New York Times.
WHAT: They were subpoenaed to appear before a grand jury about their stories on Air Force One safety issues.
WHERE: FBI agents delivered the subpoenas to the reporters’ homes late at night.
WHY: The government wants to find the people who leaked secret information about the new presidential plane.

perspectives.description: They argue that reporters should never be forced to reveal sources, because it could stop people from sharing important information that the public needs to know.
They say leaks can endanger national security, so it is their duty to find the leakers and protect the country.
They note that while press freedom is vital, courts sometimes decide that the government’s need for secrecy outweighs a journalist’s right to protect a source in certain cases.
